description: Curated registry of the world's government / standards-body instruments that set maximum (or action) levels for heavy metals in food, addressable by jurisdiction x analyte x program-category. This is the input to the Central Library's regulatory-fetch pathway (tools/central-library/lib/regulatory.mjs), which pulls the actual PDFs directly from sovereign sources -- a pathway separate from the OpenAlex/PubMed literature stack, which does not index these documents. scope_type 'horizontal' = a contaminants standard that sets limits across ALL food categories (so it is relevant to any program category); 'category-specific' = an instrument bound to a named matrix; 'assessment' = a toxicological basis document (JECFA/EFSA), not a limit instrument. pdf_url/landing_url/access/verified are refreshed by the URL-discovery agents and by the merge step; verified:false means the URL is a best-known seed not yet confirmed to resolve to the document.

instruments.body: Codex Alimentarius Commission (Food and Agriculture Organization / World Health Organization)
instruments.instrument: General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed
instruments.verify_note: This exact URL is the link FAO's own site publishes for CXS 193-1995 (confirmed via WebSearch, top result on fao.org). Automated fetchers (WebFetch, curl with browser UA) are blocked with HTTP 403 by a Cloudflare 'managed challenge' (cf-mitigated: challenge) that requires live JS execution. A real interactive browser session passed the challenge and the network trace showed the actual request returning HTTP 200 with the response handled as a file download (not an HTML error page) -- confirming the link is live and serves the genuine PDF, not a broken link. Because the automated tool could not read the bytes directly, document content/values were cross-verified against a dated mirror (isdi.org copy of the same standard, cover page reads 'Adopted in 1995. Revised in 1997, 2006, 2008, 2009. Amended in 2010, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019.'). Verified in that mirror: LEAD section (p.49-52) includes row 'Infant formula, formula for special medical purposes intended for infants and follow-up formula' = 0.01 mg/kg (as consumed; commodity standards CXS 72-1981, CXS 156-1987). ARSENIC section (p.45-46, inorganic As): Rice, husked = 0.35 mg/kg; Rice, polished = 0.20 mg/kg (general, not infant-labelled in this mirror). MERCURY (p.54, total Hg): natural mineral waters 0.001 mg/kg, salt 0.1 mg/kg (no infant row). METHYLMERCURY (p.55): species-specific ML e.g. tuna 1.2, marlin 1.7, shark 1.6 mg/kg (not infant-specific). TIN (p.56): canned foods (other than beverages) 250 mg/kg, canned beverages 150 mg/kg (no infant-specific row in this mirror). CADMIUM section (p.47-48) has no infant-formula row.
instruments.notes: The global reference standard; the biggest single gap. Sets MLs for Pb (incl. infant formula 0.01 mg/kg as-consumed), Cd, iAs in rice, MeHg in fish, Sn in canned foods. | agent: The mirror used for content verification is dated through the 2019 amendment round only; WebSearch indicates the Codex Committee on Contaminants in Food (CCCF) / CAC48 (Nov 2025) adopted further amendments (e.g., lead MLs for dried bark and dried culinary herbs) not reflected in that mirror, and the true current fao.org text could not be read directly due to the Cloudflare gate. Because of this, the analytes/infant_child_scope arrays above reflect ONLY what was directly confirmed (infant-formula lead); Codex may have additional infant-specific provisions (e.g., an infant-rice inorganic-arsenic ML paralleling the EU/UK 0.10 mg/kg figure) adopted after 2019 that this verification pass could not confirm one way or the other -- flag for a follow-up check against the live fao.org text from a real browser or a 2023-2025-dated mirror. A working free-mirror alternative (same caveat about vintage) is https://www.isdi.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/CXS-193-1995.pdf. Codex sets a Tin ML for canned foods generally (250 mg/kg) but, unlike the EU/UK, did not show a canned-infant-formula-specific Sn row in the verified mirror.

instruments.instrument: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006
instruments.verify_note: Navigated live to the EUR-Lex consolidated-text page; page title and in-document header both read '02023R0915 -- EN -- 08.10.2025 -- 006.001', confirming this is the current consolidated version (amendments through M10, Commission Regulation (EU) 2025/1891 of 17 September 2025, OJ L 1891, in force 18.9.2025 / consolidated from 8.10.2025). Extracted the full document text (123,319 characters) via the live DOM and read the complete metals annex (Section 3) verbatim. Confirmed infant/child-specific values: LEAD 3.1.24 infant/follow-on/young-child formula placed on market as powder = 0.020 mg/kg, as liquid = 0.010 mg/kg; 3.1.26 baby food / processed cereal-based food = 0.020 mg/kg. CADMIUM 3.2.17 formula powder (cow's-milk protein) = 0.010, liquid = 0.005, powder (soy) = 0.020, liquid (soy) = 0.010 mg/kg; 3.2.20 baby food/processed cereal-based = 0.040 mg/kg. INORGANIC ARSENIC (explicit heading 'Inorganic arsenic (sum of As(III) and As(V))', applies to 3.4.1-3.4.8): 3.4.1.5 rice destined for production of food for infants and young children = 0.10 mg/kg; 3.4.2 infant/follow-on/FSMP/young-child formula powder = 0.020, liquid = 0.010 mg/kg; 3.4.3 baby food = 0.020 mg/kg. TIN (inorganic) 3.5.3 canned infant/follow-on/young-child formula (excl. dried/powder) = 50 mg/kg; 3.5.4 canned baby food/processed cereal-based = 50 mg/kg. NICKEL (new Section 3.6, added by amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 of 30 July 2024, in force from 1 July 2025) 3.6.13 infant/follow-on/FSMP/young-child formula: powder (non-soy) = 0.25 mg/kg, powder (soy protein isolate) = 0.40 mg/kg, liquid = 0.10 mg/kg; 3.6.14 processed cereal-based food for infants = 3.0 mg/kg; 3.6.15 baby food = 0.50 mg/kg. Separately confirmed the PDF endpoint is live: browser network trace on https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:02023R0915-20251008 showed HTTP 202 Accepted (EUR-Lex generates PDFs on demand) followed by HTTP 200 OK, handled by the browser as a file download (consistent with a genuine PDF being served); WebFetch could not retrieve this on-demand-generated PDF directly (returned empty), which is why verification relied on the live HTML consolidated text plus the network-level 200 confirmation on the PDF endpoint. | EUR-Lex 202-blocks automated PDF generation (browser one-click works); consolidated values verified from EUR-Lex HTML. Mirror is the as-adopted 2023 OJ text (pre-2024 nickel amendment) from BCZ-CBL.
instruments.notes: Replaced Reg (EC) 1881/2006. Distinct MLs for infant formula, follow-on formula, processed cereal-based foods and baby foods (Pb, Cd, iAs, Sn, Hg via fish). Consolidated text on EUR-Lex. | agent: Mercury (total) has no infant/child-specific row in this instrument (only general fishery-product, food-supplement, and salt limits) -- excluded from analytes/infant_child_scope for that reason, per the task's scoping rule. Total arsenic is set only for salt (3.4.9, general, not infant-specific) -- also excluded. No chromium (Cr/Cr-VI) or aluminium limits exist anywhere in this instrument. IMPORTANT CROSS-JURISDICTION FINDING: the EU's current lead limit for powdered infant formula (0.020 mg/kg) is 2.5x stricter than the UK's retained-law figure (0.050 mg/kg, see uk-1881-2006-retained below) because the EU tightened Pb limits, added infant-specific inorganic-arsenic limits, and added Nickel limits entirely via amendments adopted after the UK's EU-Exit transition ended (31 Dec 2020) -- the UK has not transposed any of these. This is a material, verified divergence, not a rounding artifact. | EU 2024/1756 amendment + 2023/915 consolidated text + placing-on-market guide retrieved in the 2026-08-03 package.

instruments.body: UK Government (assimilated law; originally European Commission)
instruments.instrument: Commission Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006 of 19 December 2006 setting maximum levels for certain contaminants in foodstuffs, as it forms part of retained/assimilated EU law in the United Kingdom (Great Britain), as amended
instruments.verify_note: Fetched the PDF directly (HTTP 200, genuine 1.01 MB PDF, 29 pages read in full via the PDF reader). Document header on every page reads '02006R1881 -- EN -- 28.09.2020 -- 026.001' (i.e. consolidated through amendment M32, Commission Regulation (EU) 2020/1255). The legislation.gov.uk landing page confirms this is the 'Latest available (Revised)' version, with the note 'There are currently no known outstanding effects by UK legislation.' Confirmed infant/child-specific values, Section 3 (Metals): LEAD 3.1.2 infant formulae and follow-on formulae, powder = 0.050 mg/kg, liquid = 0.010 mg/kg; 3.1.3 processed cereal-based foods and baby foods = 0.050 mg/kg; 3.1.4 food for special medical purposes for infants, powder = 0.050, liquid = 0.010 mg/kg; 3.1.5 drinks for infants/young children, liquid or reconstituted = 0.030 mg/kg, infusion/decoction = 1.50 mg/kg. CADMIUM 3.2.19 infant/follow-on formulae: powdered cow's-milk-protein = 0.010, liquid cow's-milk = 0.005, powdered soy = 0.020, liquid soy = 0.010 mg/kg (all 'as from 1 January 2015'); 3.2.20 processed cereal-based foods/baby foods = 0.040 mg/kg. TIN (inorganic) 3.4.3 canned baby foods/processed cereal-based foods (excl. dried/powdered) = 50 mg/kg; 3.4.4 canned infant/follow-on formulae (excl. dried/powdered) = 50 mg/kg; 3.4.5 canned dietary foods for special medical purposes for infants = 50 mg/kg. ARSENIC (inorganic) 3.5.1 non-parboiled milled rice = 0.20 mg/kg; 3.5.2 parboiled/husked rice = 0.25 mg/kg; 3.5.4 rice destined for production of food for infants and young children = 0.10 mg/kg.
instruments.notes: Great Britain retained/assimilated version of 1881/2006, diverging from EU 2023/915 post-Brexit. Northern Ireland follows EU rules under the Windsor Framework. | agent: This is the UK's frozen retained-law text: the original EU Regulation (EC) 1881/2006 as it stood at the end of the Brexit transition period, consolidated with one further amendment to 28.09.2020, and not updated since. Mercury (3.3, total Hg) has no infant-specific row, same as in the EU instrument. No Nickel, Chromium, or Aluminium limits exist in this instrument at all. A follow-up WebSearch specifically confirmed the UK has NOT transposed the EU's post-Brexit tightening: 'This legislation [EU 2023/915] does not apply in GB as it was introduced after EU Exit,' and no UK statutory instrument amending contaminant metal limits was found for 2021-2025. Practical effect: GB infant-formula lead limit (0.050 mg/kg powder) is currently 2.5x less strict than the EU's current limit (0.020 mg/kg), and GB has no Nickel limit and no infant-formula-specific inorganic-arsenic limit at all, unlike the EU (see eu-2023-915 notes). This is a genuine, currently-live regulatory divergence between GB and the EU on infant-food heavy-metal limits, relevant to any HMTc cross-jurisdiction standard-setting that cites 'strictest applicable government ML.'

instruments.body: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Human Foods Program / Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition
instruments.instrument: Guidance for Industry: Action Level for Inorganic Arsenic in Rice Cereals for Infants
instruments.verify_note: GET https://www.fda.gov/media/97234/download -> HTTP 200; content-type application/pdf; content-disposition filename=ArsenicRiceGuidance_August2020.pdf; last-modified 2020-08-03; size 127,086 bytes. Full text read confirms: action level = 100 microgram per kilogram (µg/kg) / 100 ppb inorganic arsenic in infant rice cereals; final guidance dated August 2020; finalizes the April 2016 draft (81 FR 19976); docket FDA-2016-D-1099; applies to all types of infant rice cereal (white, brown, organic, conventional). Landing constituent-update page also confirmed HTTP 200.
instruments.notes: Final action level 100 micrograms/kg (100 ppb) inorganic arsenic in infant rice cereal. Part of Closer to Zero. | agent: Nonbinding guidance under 21 CFR 109.4/109.6 — not a tolerance or binding regulatory limit. FDA states it will consider the action level, among other factors, when deciding whether a specific infant rice cereal is adulterated under FD&C Act section 402(a)(1); a measured exceedance is not automatically a violation. No FDA action level exists for iAs in infant formula, non-rice infant cereals, or other infant/child foods. Sits under the broader 'Closer to Zero' action plan (landing page https://www.fda.gov/food/environmental-contaminants-food/closer-zero-reducing-childhood-exposure-contaminants-foods, confirmed HTTP 200, 2026-08-03).

instruments.body: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Human Foods Program
instruments.instrument: Guidance for Industry: Action Levels for Lead in Processed Food Intended for Babies and Young Children
instruments.verify_note: GET https://www.fda.gov/media/164684/download -> HTTP 200; content-type application/pdf; content-disposition filename=FDA-Guidance-Jan2025-LeadProcessedFoodBabyChildren-12312024.pdf; last-modified 2025-02-05; size 475,247 bytes. Full text read (pages 1-10) confirms three action levels: 10 ppb for fruits, vegetables (excluding single-ingredient root vegetables), mixtures (incl. grain- and meat-based), yogurts, custards/puddings, and single-ingredient meats; 20 ppb for single-ingredient root vegetables; 20 ppb for dry infant cereals. Final guidance dated January 2025, docket FDA-2022-D-0278. Landing search-fda-guidance-documents page also confirmed HTTP 200 directly via curl.
instruments.notes: Final Jan 2025. 10 ppb for fruits/vegetables/dry cereals; 20 ppb for root vegetables and dry cereals. Part of Closer to Zero. | agent: IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMIT: this guidance explicitly EXCLUDES infant formula and all beverages/toddler drinks (guidance footnote 2) — FDA has NOT issued a lead action level for infant formula itself; lead in juice is addressed separately by a still-DRAFT guidance (https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/draft-guidance-industry-action-levels-lead-juice), not final as of this check. Also excludes raw agricultural commodities, homemade foods, and grain-based/freeze-dried snacks (arrowroot cookies, puffs, rusks, teething biscuits) — FDA says it is still collecting snack data. Action levels benchmarked to FDA's Interim Reference Level (IRL) of 2.2 µg/day for children (updated 2022) at the 90th-percentile consumption scenario. Nonbinding guidance under 21 CFR 109.6; part of Closer to Zero. The 2025-04-21 Federal Register notice is an administrative correction, not a substantive change to the action levels.

instruments.body: Health Canada, Bureau of Chemical Safety, Food Directorate; enforced by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA)
instruments.instrument: List of Contaminants and Other Adulterating Substances in Foods — Part 2: Maximum Levels (incorporated by reference into Division 15 of the Food and Drug Regulations, C.R.C., c. 870)
instruments.reference: Incorporated by reference under B.15.001, Division 15, Food and Drug Regulations (C.R.C., c. 870); list first established 2016-05-04 (SOR/2016-74); relevant modifications NOM/ADM C-2020-2 (Lead) and NOM/ADM C-2022-2 (inorganic Arsenic)
instruments.verify_note: 2026-08-03: Health Canada publishes this only as a live HTML page (no static PDF). SerpAPI returned a wrong Natural-Health-Products guidance PDF, now rejected by the hint-guard. Retrieve values from the landing page. Confirmed: Pb in infant formula 0.01 ppm; iAs in rice-based infant foods 0.1 ppm; no Cd/Sn/Ni/Cr limits.
instruments.notes: Health Canada maintains MLs administratively (not always a single Regulation). Includes As in fruit juice/infant-relevant items; infant formula composition under the Food and Drug Regulations. | agent: Companion legacy instrument 'List of Maximum Levels for Various Chemical Contaminants in Foods' (https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/food-nutrition/food-safety/chemical-contaminants/maximum-levels-chemical-contaminants-foods.html, confirmed HTTP 200, fetched and read in full) contains ONLY a general (non-infant-specific) Mercury ML — 0.5 mg/kg in edible portion of retail fish generally, 1 mg/kg for six named species (escolar, orange roughy, marlin, fresh/frozen tuna, shark, swordfish) — with no infant/child-specific carve-out; not included as a separate record because it has no infant-specific heavy-metal entry. CONFIRMED ABSENT across BOTH Canadian lists: no regulatory maximum level exists for cadmium, tin, nickel, or chromium/Cr-VI in any food (infant or general) in Canada as of this check. General (non-infant) Lead entries in the same list (not reproduced in analytes above): beverages 0.2 ppm, condensed/evaporated milk 0.15 ppm, fruit juice/nectar 0.05 ppm, edible bone meal 10 ppm, tomato paste/sauce 1.5 ppm. Archived historical snapshots of this list exist as static HTML (e.g. .../archive004.html, dated 2018-09-16) but the CURRENT version has no equivalent static archive or PDF. | Health Canada 2019 lead-in-infant-formula proposal (HTML) retrieved in the 2026-08-03 package; the full current contaminants list stays HTML-only on canada.ca.

instruments.body: Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ); Standard made under the Food Standards Australia New Zealand Act 1991 (Cth); administered by the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
instruments.instrument: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code – Standard 1.4.1 – Contaminants and Natural Toxicants, and Schedule 19 – Maximum Levels of Contaminants and Natural Toxicants
instruments.reference: Standard 1.4.1: FRLI F2015L00408 (current compilation F2022C00972, No.2); Schedule 19: FRLI F2015L00454 (current compilation F2024C00908, No.6, up to Amendment No. 231)
instruments.verify_note: GET https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2015L00454/2024-09-13/2024-09-13/text/original/pdf -> HTTP 200; content-type application/pdf; content-disposition filename=F2024C00908.pdf; size 230,127 bytes ('Authorised Version F2024C00908 registered 21/10/2024'). Full text read confirms, in section S19-4 (Maximum levels of metal contaminants): Aluminium — infant formula, follow-on formula and special medical purpose product for infants (other than pre-term) = 0.5 mg/kg; soy-based infant formula products = 1 mg/kg; special medical purpose product for pre-term infants = 0.2 mg/kg (entry inserted 13 Sept 2024, Amendment No. 231). Lead — infant formula products = 0.02 mg/kg (amended FROM 0.01 mg/kg TO 0.02 mg/kg on 13 Sept 2024, same Amendment No. 231, per the in-document Amendment History table). Companion operative Standard 1.4.1 PDF independently verified: GET https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2015L00408/2022-09-01/2022-09-01/text/original/pdf -> HTTP 200, filename=F2022C00972.pdf, 440,458 bytes, 'compilation No. 2 of Standard 1.4.1 as in force on 1 September 2022'.
instruments.notes: Schedule 19 carries the numeric MLs. Standard 2.9.1/2.9.2 cover infant formula and infant foods composition. Register of Legislation serves the PDF. | agent: FLAG: Schedule 19's infant-formula Lead maximum level was RAISED (loosened) from 0.01 mg/kg to 0.02 mg/kg effective 13 September 2024 (Food Standards (Proposal P1028 – Infant Formula Products – Consequential Amendments) Variation, FRLI F2024L01151) — confirmed directly from the Schedule's own Amendment History table, not inferred. A 5-year transitional window (13 Sept 2024 to 13 Sept 2029) permits sale under either the pre- or post-amendment Code. Standard 1.4.1 itself carries no infant-specific numeric limit; it is the operative clause (section 1.4.1-3) that gives Schedule 19's table legal effect, plus a 'background calculation factor' (CF) used only when apportioning MLs across multi-ingredient foods: Pb 0.01 mg/kg, Cd 0.005 mg/kg (section 1.4.1-3(3)) — these are blending-formula constants, not food-specific maximum levels, so Cd is not listed in the analytes array above. No FSANZ infant-formula-specific limit exists for Cadmium, Arsenic (Schedule 19 has only a general cereal-grains total-As level of 1 mg/kg and crustacea/fish/mollusc/seaweed inorganic-As levels of 1-2 mg/kg, neither infant-specific), Mercury (fish/salt only, not infant-specific), Nickel, or Chromium/Cr-VI. Tin (250 mg/kg, all canned foods) could apply to canned infant purees/foods but is not an infant-specific entry.

instruments.body: National Health Commission (NHC) and State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR)
instruments.instrument: National Food Safety Standard — Maximum Levels of Contaminants in Foods
instruments.verify_note: WebFetch + local PDF read confirmed the gdgrain.gd.gov.cn PDF is the genuine GB 2762-2022 full text: cover page reads 'GB 2762—2022 食品安全国家标准 食品中污染物限量', issued 2022-06-30, implemented 2023-06-30, jointly issued by NHC and SAMR, superseding GB 2762-2017. Read pages 1-15 directly and confirmed infant-specific rows: Pb – infant formula (婴幼儿配方食品) 0.08 mg/kg as solid product with an 8:1 liquid-to-solid conversion factor, infant complementary food (婴幼儿辅助食品) 0.2 mg/kg; Cd – infant cereal complementary food 0.06 mg/kg; total Hg – infant canned complementary food 0.02 mg/kg; As – infant cereal complementary food inorganic-As 0.2 (0.3 with added algae), infant canned complementary food inorganic-As 0.1 (0.3 with aquatic/animal-liver ingredients), milk powder/modified milk powder total-As 0.5; Sn – infant formula & infant complementary food 50 mg/kg (vs. 250 general food / 150 beverages). Did not independently fetch the primary CFSA query platform (sppt.cfsa.net.cn) or an NHC page specific to the 2022 announcement in this session (an nhc.gov.cn URL attempt returned HTTP 412); relying on multiple concordant secondary Chinese industry/standards sites for confirmation that gdgrain's copy matches the authentic, currently in-force text.
instruments.notes: Original title: 食品安全国家标准 食品中污染物限量. Sets Pb, Cd, As (total + inorganic for rice), Hg (total + methyl), Sn, Cr, Ni. Official standard is published free by NHC but often mirrored; English translations circulate. Effective 2023-06-30. | agent: 原文标题: 食品安全国家标准 食品中污染物限量 (GB 2762-2022), 国家卫生健康委员会 + 国家市场监督管理总局 发布. CRITICAL CURRENCY NOTE: GB 2762-2025 was published 2025-09-25 (NHC/SAMR Announcement No. 6 of 2025, see nhc.gov.cn/sps/c100088/202509/5dc5e1e2b26d4d27a7913b9e71bbe931.shtml) and takes effect 2026-09-02, at which point GB 2762-2022 is explicitly abolished (废止) — as of today (2026-08-03) GB 2762-2022 is still the in-force text but supersession is under one month away; re-verify before citing after 2026-09-02. GB 2762-2025's (unverified, paid) English preview: chinesestandard.net/PDF-EN/GB2762-2025EN-P06P-H5002H-529904.pdf. GB 2762-2022 does NOT cover aluminium (Al) at all and covers only total chromium (no Cr-VI speciation); Cr appears only under the general 'milk powder and modified milk powder' row (2.0 mg/kg), not explicitly named for the infant-formula category, and Ni appears only for hydrogenated vegetable oils — neither is meaningfully infant-specific in this standard. ENGLISH TRANSLATION IS PAID: both codeofchina.com and chinesestandard.net charge ~US$285 (email delivery) for the full English version; the free preview shows only the lead (Pb) table in English. Backup/summary source: USDA FAS GAIN has prior China contaminants-standard summaries (e.g. fas.usda.gov/data/china-china-s-maximum-levels-contaminants-foods) though none located this session is a line-by-line summary of the 2022 text specifically.

instruments.body: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) for the Milk Ordinance; Consumer Affairs Agency (CAA, 消費者庁) for Notification No. 370 since a 2024-04-01 jurisdictional transfer from MHLW
instruments.instrument: Ministerial Ordinance Concerning Compositional Standards, etc. for Milk and Milk Products (governs formulated/infant milk powder compositionally); Specifications and Standards for Foods, Food Additives, etc. under the Food Sanitation Act (the general contaminants/specifications framework)
instruments.reference: MHLW Ordinance No. 52 of 1951 (乳等省令), as amended through 2024-03-29; Notification No. 370 of 1959 (厉告示第三百七十号), as amended
instruments.verify_note: WebFetch of the landing_url confirmed it is the current official text of MHLW Ordinance No. 52 (1951), amended through 2024-03-29. Its article on 調製粉乳 (formulated milk powder) specifies only compositional (≥50.0% milk solids) and microbiological requirements — no lead/arsenic/tin/cadmium/mercury limit appears in the accessible text. Separately, direct PDF read of mhlw.go.jp/topics/bukyoku/iyaku/kigu/dl/5.pdf (an official, current excerpt of Notification No. 370) confirmed it contains heavy-metal migration limits, but only for TOYS §4 (including rubber baby pacifiers: Pb ≤90 µg/g, Cd ≤75 µg/g, As ≤25 µg/g eluate) — a child-product-safety standard, not a food-contaminant standard. Also fetched CAA's current food-category standards index (caa.go.jp/policies/policy/standards_evaluation/other/category), which lists ~18 per-food categories with dedicated heavy-metal/contaminant provisions (soft drinks, canned/metal-container foods, fish products, grains, etc.) and confirmed milk/dairy/infant-formula is NOT among them, consistent with dairy being carved out to the separate Milk Ordinance. No consolidated numeric heavy-metal MRL table for infant formula or infant/child foods was found in Japanese law comparable to China's GB 2762 or Korea's Food Code, despite a thorough multi-angle search (direct ordinance text, e-Gov official law portal, CAA per-food index, MHLW notification excerpts, FFCR/JETRO translations, USDA GAIN reports).
instruments.notes: Japan regulates metals via food-type specifications rather than a single contaminants table. Powdered infant formula standards under the milk ordinance. English translations partial; japaneselawtranslation.go.jp may carry a version. | agent: 原文名称: 乳及び乳製品の成分規格等に関する省令 (昭和26年12月27日厚生省令第52号) and 食品、添加物等の規格基準 (昭和34年厚生省告示第370号). HONEST STRUCTURAL FINDING (not a research gap): Japan does not appear to operate a consolidated, numeric heavy-metal maximum-level table for infant formula or infant/child foods analogous to China's GB 2762 or Korea's Food Code — hence empty analytes/speciation/pdf_url above are a substantive finding, not a placeholder. What DOES exist and is heavy-metal-adjacent in Japanese food law: (1) cadmium in rice ≤0.4 mg/kg polished rice, an individual Article 11 standard harmonized with the 2006 Codex value (predecessor: <1.0 ppm brown rice from 1970) — general food-supply standard, relevant only indirectly as an input constraint on rice-based infant cereal, not infant-specific; (2) arsenic/lead 'not detected' or low-ppm standards for mineral water and soft drinks; (3) tin dissolution limits for metal-can beverage containers; (4) the toy-safety heavy-metal migration limits noted above, which cover rubber pacifiers as a child PRODUCT (not a food); (5) the Food Sanitation Act's general Article 6 prohibition on injurious/harmful food, which appears to be the operative catch-all for infant-formula heavy-metal safety in the absence of a published ppm ceiling. The 1955 Morinaga arsenic-contaminated-infant-formula poisoning incident (over 12,000 infants affected, ~130 deaths) is the direct historical reason this topic receives elevated scrutiny in Japan, but that scrutiny appears to run through manufacturer self-testing and Article 6 rather than a published numeric standard. FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATION: check for a non-binding MHLW/CAA guidance notice (事務連絡 or 通知, a softer instrument type than a 告示) specifically addressing arsenic or lead in infant formula post-1955; this document type was not searched exhaustively and would not match this schema's 'binding standard' framing cleanly if found. SECONDARY/BACKUP SOURCES: JETRO's English compilation of the food specifications (~2010 vintage, likely structurally accurate but not verified current in exact wording): jetro.go.jp/ext_images/en/reports/regulations/pdf/foodext2010e.pdf; FFCR (Japan Food Chemical Research Foundation) hosts translated materials at ffcr.or.jp/en/ (the specific 'Part II.pdf' found during this research is a 2006 seminar background paper, NOT the regulation text, and should not be cited as the standard itself); USDA FAS GAIN Japan FAIRS Country Reports (fas.usda.gov/data/japan-food-and-agricultural-import-regulations-and-standards-country-report) give a general English framework overview but do not tabulate infant-formula heavy-metal limits either. Japan's official consolidated law portal (e-Gov, laws.e-gov.go.jp) hosts the current Milk Ordinance text at https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/document?lawid=326M50000100052_20210601_501M60000100087 but this session's automated fetch could not render its full text (likely JS-driven); a human or a headless-browser pass could check it directly as a final confirmation step. | Fetched PDF is the Milk Ordinance (MHW Ord. No. 52/1951) English translation = compositional standards; Japan has no single consolidated heavy-metal MRL table for infant formula (Notification 370 moved to the Consumer Affairs Agency 2024-04-01).

instruments.body: Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS)
instruments.instrument: Korean Food Code — Article 2 (Common Standards & Specifications for General Foods, §5 Heavy Metal) and Article 3 (Standards and Specifications for Foods Labeled and Sold for Infants and Young Children, the Elderly, or as Meal Replacements)
instruments.reference: MFDS Notice No. 2026-1 (current consolidated Food Code); heavy-metal figures verified against MFDS's official English translation of Article 2
instruments.verify_note: WebFetch + local PDF read of the mfds.go.kr PDF confirmed genuine English text 'Article 2. Common Standards & Specifications for General Foods' with a '5) Heavy Metal' section giving: marine fish & shellfish (live-weight basis) total Hg ≤0.5 mg/kg (except deep-sea fish/tuna/spearfish, MeHg ≤1.0 mg/kg for those), Pb ≤0.5 mg/kg; shellfish/mollusca total Hg ≤0.5, Pb ≤2.0, Cd ≤2.0 mg/kg; agricultural products (raw basis) Pb and Cd limits for rice/corn/soybean/red-bean/sweet potato/potato/chinese cabbage/spinach/leek/radish (e.g. rice Pb 0.2, Cd 0.2 mg/kg). Could NOT confirm within this pass whether these figures match MFDS Notice No. 2026-1 exactly or reflect a slightly earlier translation vintage (no notice number/date is printed on the PDF pages read). Could NOT locate or fetch the Article 3 (infant/young-children-specific) English PDF in this session despite targeted searching; its existence and title are confirmed via MFDS Notice 2018-98 (effective 2020-01-01, which introduced the infants/young-children/elderly chapter) and via ChemLinked's description of the current Food Code structure, but no direct URL for it was found.
instruments.notes: Food Code Chapter on general/individual standards carries Pb/Cd/As/Hg/Sn limits, including a category for foods for infants and young children. English version via MFDS/foodsafetykorea. | agent: 원문 명칭: 식품의 기준 및 규격 (통칭 '식품공전', 'Food Code'), 식품의약품안전처(MFDS) 고시. Current consolidated notice as of 2026-08-03 is MFDS Notice No. 2026-1 (food.chemlinked.com/database/view/6733); the Code is amended very frequently — dozens of numbered notices per year (examples seen this session: 2022-7, 2022-16, 2024-22, 2024-71, 2026-1), plus further draft revisions (2026-310 / 2026-311, comment period through 2026-08-31) — so any cited figure should be re-checked against the live text at foodsafetykorea.go.kr/foodcode/ before use in a defensibility context. Structure confirmed: Article 1 General Provisions; Article 2 Common Standards & Specifications for General Foods (heavy-metal section used here); Article 3 Standards and Specifications for Foods Labeled and Sold for Infants and Young Children, the Elderly, or as Meal Replacements (this is almost certainly where infant-formula-specific Pb/Cd/As limits live — not independently retrieved this session; flagged as the priority follow-up). A broader (but likely ~2018–2019-vintage) English deposit of the fuller code, whose General Provisions/Common Standards text matches the MFDS PDF read here, sits at FAO's legal database: faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/kor190522.pdf — useful as a fuller backup document but not confirmed current. Korean-language primary source (official, browsable by chapter): foodsafetykorea.go.kr/foodcode/. Backup English secondary summary: USDA FAS GAIN 'Food and Agricultural Import Regulations and Standards' report for Korea, e.g. apps.fas.usda.gov/newgainapi/api/report/downloadreportbyfilename?filename=Food+and+Agricultural+Import+Regulations+and+Standards+Report_Seoul_Korea+-+Republic+of_3-22-2019.pdf. Web-search snippets (NOT independently verified against a fetched primary document this session, so excluded from the 'analytes'/'speciation' fields above) suggested inorganic-arsenic limits around 0.2 mg/kg for grains generally and 0.35 mg/kg for brown rice — plausible and consistent with regional norms, but pending first-hand confirmation.

instruments.body: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
instruments.instrument: Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Regulations, 2011 — consolidated Compendium, Version IX
instruments.reference: FSS (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Regulations, 2011, regulation 2.1 (Metal Contaminants); consolidated Compendium version IX dated 03.02.2026
instruments.verify_note: pdf_url returns HTTP 200 to curl/WebFetch but the body is FSSAI's React SPA shell (title 'FSSAI - Food Safety and Standards Authority of India', ~750 bytes), not the PDF — the fssai.gov.in upload path sits behind a bot-detection/WAF challenge (Set-Cookie: TS0191b667... Imperva-style token) that blocked every direct-fetch attempt in this session, including via a real browser navigation (redirected to the homepage). Google's own search index has independently crawled this exact URL and returned matching regulatory text ('Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, toxins and...' title, 'Crop contaminant' definition), which corroborates the file is genuine and current (Version IX) even though this session could not independently re-fetch its bytes. Not re-attempted further to avoid trying to bypass bot-detection. 2026-08-04: local primary-source copy on file in the 2026-08-03 package.
instruments.notes: Metal limits table sets Pb, Cd, As, Hg, Sn (methyl mercury for fish); specific tighter limits for infant milk substitutes and infant foods. Compendium PDF hosted by FSSAI. | agent: FSSAI's own regulation table is titled 'METAL CONTAMINANTS' (reg. 2.1) inside Chapter 2 'Contaminants, Toxins and Residues'. A verified WORKING mirror on an FSSAI subdomain, https://jaivikbharat.fssai.gov.in/pdf/Compendium_Contaminants_Regulations.pdf (HTTP 200, application/pdf, 1,101,127 bytes — confirmed by direct download + pdftotext), is stamped throughout as 'Version–II (18.08.2017)', i.e. an OUTDATED snapshot roughly nine versions behind the current compendium (Version IX, 2026). That verified 2017 text gives, under the 'Infant Milk substitute and Infant foods' category: Lead 0.2 mg/kg (item 1), Cadmium 0.1 mg/kg (item 6). It shows Arsenic (item 3), Tin (item 4), Mercury (item 7), Methylmercury (item 8), Chromium (item 9) and Nickel (item 10) sections for OTHER food categories (vinegar, soft drinks, fish, salt, mineral water, hydrogenated oils, etc.) but no infant-specific row for any of those five in this 2017 text. Secondary regulatory-intelligence sources (foodsafetyhelpline.com and others, unverified against primary text) report FSSAI now also sets an inorganic-arsenic limit of 0.1 mg/kg for infant rice cereal/rice-based infant food — plausibly a post-2017 amendment not present in the verified Version-II mirror; could not independently confirm the exact clause. CAUTION — one web-search AI summary claimed 'lead in infant formula is set at 0.02 mg/kg,' which directly conflicts with the 0.2 mg/kg this session verified in the primary 2017 text; 0.02 mg/kg is also, suspiciously, exactly Brazil's NEW post-2025 infant-food lead limit (see the Brazil entry), so this looks like a cross-jurisdiction conflation in that secondary source rather than a real FSSAI value. Treat 0.2 mg/kg (Pb) and 0.1 mg/kg (Cd) as the verified-but-possibly-stale figures, and the current Version IX compendium as the thing to re-check before citing a number in the wiki. USDA FAS GAIN backup: https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/india-more-amendments-contaminants-toxins-and-residues-regulations (returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch in this session, so its content is unconfirmed; listed as a lead only). No aluminium entry found anywhere in the metals table; zinc was reportedly proposed for removal from the same table (unconfirmed substance). | Local FSS Contaminants Regulations 2011 PDF retrieved in the 2026-08-03 package — backs the bot-blocked fssai.gov.in URL.

instruments.body: Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (ANVISA), Ministério da Saúde
instruments.instrument: Resolução da Diretoria Colegiada (RDC) nº 722, de 1º de julho de 2022 (general principles, scope and analytical methods for maximum tolerated limits — LMT — of contaminants in food; revokes RDC nº 487/2021, which had replaced RDC nº 42/2013); numeric LMT tables set by the companion Instrução Normativa (IN) nº 160, de 1º de julho de 2022 (which itself consolidated and revoked IN nº 88/2021, IN nº 115/2021 and IN nº 152/2022), as amended by IN nº 351, de 18 de março de 2025
instruments.reference: RDC nº 722/2022 (DOU nº 126, 6 jul. 2022, Seção 1); IN nº 160/2022 (Anexo I — metais); IN nº 351/2025 (altera Anexo I da IN 160/2022); base Mercosul: MERCOSUL/GMC/RES. Nº 12/11 as amended by Res. GMC Nº 18/21
instruments.verify_note: pdf_url confirmed: HTTP 200, content-type application/pdf, 517,838 bytes, last-modified 2022-07-06. Downloaded and ran pdftotext: text matches RDC 722 exactly — 'Art. 1º Esta Resolução dispõe sobre os limites máximos tolerados (LMT) de contaminantes em alimentos...', 'Art. 12. Fica revogada a Resolução de Diretoria Colegiada - RDC nº 487, de 26 de [2021]...', 'Art. 13. Esta Resolução entra em vigor no dia 1° de julho de 2022.' Note the mirror file is actually the full DOU Seção 1 gazette page for 6 jul. 2022 (it also contains RDC 724 on sugar/cocoa immediately after RDC 722's Art. 205/signature block), so RDC 722 itself is the first ~200 lines. A second free-mirror, https://nutrisafety.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Resolução-RDC-n°-722-de-01-de-julho-de-2022-LMT-Contaminantes-em-Alimentos.pdf, was independently confirmed the same way (HTTP 200, application/pdf, 249,048 bytes). Could NOT get a clean official gov.br/in.gov.br PDF: two gov.br/agricultura mirror URLs for IN 160/2022 returned HTTP 403 Forbidden; the AnvisaLegis official database page (anvisalegis.datalegis.net) returned HTTP 403 with 'cf-mitigated: challenge' (Cloudflare bot-challenge) — not pursued further, no attempt made to bypass it; the official in.gov.br DOU page for IN 351/2025 (https://www.in.gov.br/en/web/dou/-/instrucao-normativa-in-n-351-de-18-de-marco-de-2025-618776799) hung/timed out on both WebFetch and curl. The official gov.br/anvisa LANDING page (used as landing_url above) IS directly accessible and confirms RDC 722/2022 as current.
instruments.notes: Original title: Limites maximos tolerados (LMT) de contaminantes inorganicos em alimentos. Replaced RDC 42/2013; paired with IN 88/2021. Aligns with Mercosur GMC resolutions. Published in the Diario Oficial da Uniao. | agent: RDC 722/2022 is the FRAMEWORK act only (definitions, scope, methods of analysis, general principles) — it does not itself carry a per-food numeric table. The operative numeric limits (including all infant-food rows) live in Instrução Normativa (IN) nº 160/2022 Anexo I, which is a distinct legal instrument that was itself amended on 18 March 2025 by IN nº 351/2025. Per multiple regulatory-intelligence write-ups (Food Safety Brazil, Regoola, Fukuma Advogados — none of them primary/official, cross-checked against each other), IN 351/2025's single most-cited change is reducing the lead limit for 'alimentos à base de cereais para alimentação infantil (lactentes e crianças de primeira infância)' from 0.05 mg/kg to 0.02 mg/kg, with a 6-month compliance window (to ~18 Sept 2025) for metals/mycotoxins and 12 months (to ~18 Mar 2026) for the newly added Annex III contaminants. A cached full-text view of IN 160/2022 (as originally published, i.e. BEFORE the 2025 amendment) via legisweb.com.br (https://www.legisweb.com.br/legislacao/?id=437382 — a private legal-database aggregator, may be subscription-gated on live browsing) gave these original Anexo I figures for infant-scoped rows: Lead, cereal-based infant food = 0.05 mg/kg (now 0.02 mg/kg post-2025); Cadmium, cereal-based infant food = 0.05 mg/kg; Arsenic (inorganic only), cereal-based infant food = 0.15 mg/kg; Tin (inorganic only), canned infant foods = 50 mg/kg; no infant-specific entry found for mercury. These IN160/351 figures are SECONDARY-sourced (not independently verified against an official ANVISA/DOU PDF in this session) — flag for re-verification before wiki citation. Mercosul lineage: IN 88/2021 (the anchor instrument named in the original research brief) internalized MERCOSUL/GMC/RES. Nº 12/11 ('Reglamento Técnico Mercosur sobre Límites Máximos de Contaminantes Inorgánicos'), later amended by Res. GMC 18/21 (Oct. 2021, arsenic limit for rice); IN 88/2021 was itself revoked/consolidated into IN 160/2022 (effective 1 Sept 2022) with, per secondary sources, no substantive change to limits at that step (numbering/consolidation only) — the substantive change came later via IN 351/2025. Secondary sources also indicate Mercosur-level work is underway to revoke and replace GMC 12/11 + GMC 18/21 with a new consolidated resolution on metallic/metalloid contaminants; not yet confirmed as adopted. | Fetched PDF is RDC 722/2022 (framework + repeals, DOU). The numeric metal limit TABLES are in IN 160/2022 (Anexo I), amended by IN 351/2025 (infant-cereal Pb cut 0.05->0.02 mg/kg) — retrieve IN 160/2022 separately for the values. | ANVISA IN 88/2021 (English) retrieved in the 2026-08-03 package — carries the numeric metal LMTs paired with RDC 722/2022.

instruments.instrument: GSO 193:2021 — Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (Gulf Technical Regulation, 1st edition, approved 1 July 2021; supersedes GSO CODEX STAN 193:2008; adapted from Codex Alimentarius CXS 193-1995)
instruments.verify_note: No free pdf_url exists to verify. The GSO store landing page itself was fetched and confirmed: title 'Contaminants and toxins in food and feed', Gulf Technical Regulation, 1st edition (current), approved 01 July 2021, priced 285 currency units (English, 71 pages) / 310 (Arabic, 95 pages), 'Add to cart' / 'Download Preview' options present — no free full-text download. The store's own 'Download Preview' resolves to an official-looking preview render (gso-sims-preview-doc-aws.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/gso-193-2021-en.html) that was fetched and contains only the cover page, bilingual (Arabic/English) foreword, table of contents and scope/references sections — not the actual maximum-level annex tables, so the infant_child_scope and analyte list above are inferred from GSO 193's stated Codex-193 lineage and general subject matter, NOT independently confirmed against GSO's own annex text.
instruments.notes: GSO standards are typically sold via the GSO Store, so expect manual retrieval. A USDA FAS GAIN report often summarizes the Gulf metal limits as a free secondary source. | agent: Sold only via the GSO Standards Store (and mirrored at national-adopter storefronts, e.g. Bahrain's bsmd.moic.gov.bh and Oman's dgsm.gso.org.sa, same price). A newer draft, GSO TC05-SC2/FDS1 193:2025 (prepared by Saudi SASO), is at Final Draft Stage (FDS) per the GSO projects tracker (https://www.gso.org.sa/sp/projects/34668?lang=en) as of this session — NOT yet approved or published, so GSO 193:2021 remains the current in-force instrument. Because GSO 193 is explicitly modelled on Codex Alimentarius CXS 193-1995 ('General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed'), the free, official Codex text is the closest available free proxy for likely-overlapping scope/limits, though GSO's actual regional annex may diverge — verified working at https://www.fao.org/fileadmin/user_upload/livestockgov/documents/1_CXS_193e.pdf (HTTP 200, application/pdf, 1,113,869 bytes) and a 2015-updated edition at https://www.fao.org/input/download/standards/17/CXS_193e_2015.pdf (not independently re-verified this session). USDA FAS GAIN backup, confirmed working (HTTP 200, application/pdf, 1,032,845 bytes): 'FAIRS Country Report Annual' for Saudi Arabia, report SA2025-0013 — https://apps.fas.usda.gov/newgainapi/api/Report/DownloadReportByFileName?fileName=FAIRS+Country+Report+Annual_Riyadh_Saudi+Arabia_SA2025-0013.pdf — discusses GSO 193:2021 and the broader Saudi/GCC contaminants framework (references Saudi's practice of adopting the strictest of Codex/EU/US limits when no GSO-specific limit exists) but is a general-purpose trade-regulatory digest, not a substitute for the standard's own tables. GSO CODEX STAN 193:2008 is the directly superseded prior edition (also sold, not fetched). | GSO contaminants DRAFT 2019 (33p) retrieved in the 2026-08-03 package; the sold GSO 193:2021 final still needs purchase. USDA GAIN Saudi FAIRS 2022 summarizes the Gulf limits.

instruments.body: Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)
instruments.instrument: JECFA toxicological evaluations of lead, cadmium, inorganic arsenic and (methyl)mercury — WHO Food Additives Series No. 64 ('Safety evaluation of certain food additives and contaminants,' 73rd JECFA meeting, Geneva, 8–17 June 2010: Lead and Cadmium addenda); WHO Technical Report Series No. 959 ('Evaluation of certain contaminants in food,' 72nd JECFA meeting, Rome, 16–25 Feb. 2010: inorganic Arsenic and Mercury); WHO Technical Report Series No. 922 ('Evaluation of certain food additives and contaminants,' 61st JECFA meeting, Rome, 10–19 June 2003: Methylmercury)
instruments.reference: WHO Food Additives Series 64 / TRS-equivalent (73rd JECFA, publ. 2011, ISBN 978-92-4-166064-8); WHO Technical Report Series 959 (72nd JECFA, publ. 2011, ISBN 978-92-4-120959-5); WHO Technical Report Series 922 (61st JECFA, publ. 2004, ISBN 92-4-120922-4)
instruments.verify_note: pdf_url confirmed by direct download: HTTP 200, content-type application/pdf, Content-Disposition filename='9789241660648_eng.pdf', 2,949,350 bytes, 75 pages (a bare HEAD request without a Referer returned an HTTP 500 from the DSpace/IRIS REST API — a full GET with a standard browser User-Agent and Referer, i.e. what any real browser sends, returns 200 cleanly). pdftotext confirms front matter 'WHO FOOD ADDITIVES SERIES: 64 ... Prepared by the Seventy-third meeting of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA), World Health Organization, Geneva, 2011' and table-of-contents entries 'Cadmium (addendum)' and 'Lead (addendum)', plus body sections titled 'CADMIUM (addendum)' with cadmium occurrence/excretion data. Companion documents independently verified the same way: WHO TRS 959 (72nd meeting) at https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/cf852bd0-d911-4d9d-a3d1-3b022827a7ec/content — HTTP 200, application/pdf, filename 'WHO_TRS_959_eng.pdf', 1,750,364 bytes, 34 pages; pdftotext confirms sections '3.2 Arsenic' and '3.5 Mercury'. WHO TRS 922 (61st meeting) at https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/34f83d75-1bc5-4480-b245-c2076fac96f5/content — HTTP 200, application/pdf, filename 'WHO_TRS_922.pdf', 1,034,374 bytes, 188 pages; pdftotext confirms section '7.2 Methylmercury' with the PTWI derivation narrative.
instruments.notes: Not a maximum-level instrument -- the health basis behind them (Pb BMDL withdrawn PTWI; Cd PTMI 25 ug/kg-bw/month; iAs BMDL0.5; MeHg PTWI 1.6 ug/kg-bw). Underpins the 'no established safe threshold' framing for Tier 1 toxics. | agent: This is the toxicological BASIS, not a maximum-level-setting instrument (per the research brief's own framing) — hence status 'assessment'. One JECFA meeting does not cover all four analytes, so this entry synthesizes three: (1) 73rd meeting (2010, publ. 2011, primary pdf_url above) — LEAD: the existing PTWI of 25 µg/kg bw/week was WITHDRAWN as no longer health-protective, with no replacement single guidance value; the Committee instead used a benchmark-dose/margin-of-exposure approach against BMDL01/BMDL10 values for IQ loss, systolic blood pressure and chronic kidney disease endpoints in the dose-response range of typical dietary exposures. CADMIUM: the prior PTWI of 7 µg/kg bw/week was replaced with a Provisional Tolerable MONTHLY Intake (PTMI) of 25 µg/kg bw/month (≈0.83 µg/kg bw/day), reflecting cadmium's long biological half-life; a urinary-cadmium excretion threshold of 5.24 µg/g creatinine was adopted as the nephrotoxicity reference point. (2) 72nd meeting (Feb 2010, publ. 2011, WHO TRS 959) — INORGANIC ARSENIC: the prior PTWI of 15 µg/kg bw/week (≈2.1 µg/kg bw/day) was WITHDRAWN as being in the same range as the newly derived BMDL0.5 (dose associated with 0.5% extra incidence of lung cancer) of 3.0 µg/kg bw/day (range 2–7 µg/kg bw/day across dietary exposure estimates), so the old PTWI could no longer be considered protective. INORGANIC MERCURY: PTWI revised to 4 µg/kg bw/week (replacing the older total-mercury PTWI of 5 µg/kg bw/week, which was withdrawn and explicitly said to no longer apply to non-fish dietary mercury exposure). (3) 61st meeting (2003, publ. 2004, WHO TRS 922) — METHYLMERCURY: PTWI of 1.6 µg/kg bw/week (down from an earlier 3.3 µg/kg bw/week), based on epidemiological cohorts of fish-eating populations and developmental neurotoxicity endpoints; this value has not been revised since and remains JECFA's current MeHg guidance. Free-mirror/navigation alternatives: the JECFA online database (https://apps.who.int/food-additives-contaminants-jecfa-database/) is a searchable per-chemical index into all meeting outputs; inchem.org hosts older monographs as stable HTML/PDF (e.g. methylmercury monograph https://www.inchem.org/documents/jecfa/jecmono/v52je01.htm, WHO Food Additives Series 52); short 'Summary and Conclusions' (SC) documents exist for many individual meetings on cdn.who.int (e.g. jecfa91, jecfa96 patterns confirmed reachable) but a working direct link specific to JECFA/72/SC or JECFA/73/SC was not confirmed in this session — the full meeting reports above were used instead and are more complete anyway.

source_packages.description: External regulatory-gathering package: 11-jurisdiction infant/child-food heavy-metal limits — 30+ primary-source PDFs/HTML, extracted text, a 141-row structured limits JSON, and an 11-jurisdiction synthesis.
source_packages.validation_status: UNVALIDATED. The 141-row limits JSON was spot-checked against the synthesis but NOT reconciled against the primary PDFs; do not feed it into HMTc standards (Method v2.0) before validation. Known discrepancy: Codex Pb infant-formula reads 0.02 mg/kg here vs 0.01 in some sources — resolve against Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf.
